hook: Shumbha says the goddess fights with borrowed strength; she answers that she is alone, and all the goddesses go back into her

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, Raktabija multiplied with every drop of blood, until Kali caught each drop before it could land. Did you catch a first annoyed thought before it grew? Day one thousand seventy.

It's an old insult. You didn't really do it. Somebody did it for you. In the ninth chapter, Nishumbha, the younger brother, falls. The goddess strikes him down, and even then, the text says, another figure rises out of his chest shouting stop, and she laughs and cuts off its head. Now only Shumbha is left. His brother is dead. His army is gone. And in the tenth chapter, he looks across the field at the goddess surrounded by Kali and the other goddesses, and he throws the insult at her. In paraphrase: don't be so proud, Durga. You fight leaning on the strength of others. What she says next is the line this chapter turns on.
screen: `NISHUMBHA FALLS.` → `ONLY SHUMBHA IS LEFT.` → `YOU FIGHT WITH OTHERS' STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: The goddess answers, in paraphrase: I am alone here in the world. Who else is there besides me? Look, you fool. These are my own powers, going back into me. And they do. Brahmani on her swan, the goddess of Shiva's trident, the goddess on Garuda, the boar-faced one, the lion-faced one, all of them, the text says, enter the goddess's body. And the field is suddenly empty except for two figures. Shumbha, and Ambika, alone. Think about what that does to everything we've read. All along the goddess has seemed to have helpers: Kali from her brow, goddesses from the gods' bodies, troops from her own breath. Shumbha took them for allies, outside help. The goddess's answer is that there never was anyone else. In her words, every one of them was her own power, in another form. Then the last fight. The two of them battle with every weapon, then with bare hands. Shumbha seizes her and leaps into the sky, and they fight there, in the air, with nothing to stand on. At last she whirls him around and throws him to the ground, and as he rushes at her one last time, she pierces his chest with her spear. He falls, and the text describes the whole world going calm. The rivers run in their courses again. The winds blow gently. The sun shines clear. Hindu teachers read the line in more than one way. Some hear in it a teaching about the one goddess behind every form of the divine. Others hear it more simply, as the story saying who she is. The text itself just shows it: the goddesses walk back into her, and she stands alone.
screen: `I AM ALONE HERE IN THE WORLD.` · `THE GODDESSES GO BACK INTO HER.` · `THE MANY WERE ALWAYS ONE.` · `A FIGHT IN THE SKY, THEN STILLNESS.` · then, large: `WHO ELSE IS THERE BESIDES ME?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: after the battle. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind something that ended recently: a long task, a hard conversation, a worry that came to nothing. Don't replay it. Notice instead what came after it, the quiet. Let the breath run in its own course, the way the text says the rivers did. Let the shoulders loosen, then the jaw, then the hands. If you pray, you can rest in God, or the goddess, in the words you already use. If you don't, let the stillness be enough. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its ninth and tenth chapters: the two brothers fall, and the goddess answers, I am alone here in the world; who else is there besides me?
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Today, when one hard thing ends, a call, a chore, a conversation, give yourself one breath to notice what goes quiet. Day one thousand seventy.

howItsDone: The goddess's words to Shumbha in the tenth chapter of the Devi Mahatmya are recited as part of the whole text, and some Shakta teachers cite them when explaining that the many goddesses are forms of one goddess.

fork.setup: you're the goddess. Shumbha says you only win because others fight for you. what do you do?
options: say you are alone in the world, and take your powers back into yourself.
ignore him and keep fighting with all of them.
fork.reveal: she says, in paraphrase: I am alone here in the world; who else is there besides me? and every goddess enters her body. only Ambika stands.

original.note: Sanskrit: ekaivāhaṃ jagaty atra, 'I am alone here in the world,' the goddess's answer to Shumbha.

trapdoor: what you thought: a goddess who wins with a team.
what it means: every helper was her own power; when Shumbha calls them borrowed, they go back into her and she stands alone.
what a scholar hears: chapter 10, ekaivāhaṃ jagaty atra dvitīyā kā mamāparā, a verse Shakta readers cite for one goddess in many forms.

notes: Chapters 9 and 10 paraphrased. Ch. 9: Nishumbha struck down; from his heart another figure emerges crying 'stop!'; the goddess laughs and cuts off its head. Ch. 10: Shumbha's taunt (balāvalepād duṣṭe tvaṃ mā durge garvam āvaha / anyāsāṃ balam āśritya yuddhyase): her answer ekaivāhaṃ jagaty atra dvitīyā kā mamāparā / paśyaitā duṣṭa mayy eva viśantyo madvibhūtayaḥ; the goddesses enter her body and Ambika alone remains; the fight in the sky; she throws him down and pierces him with her spear; nature becomes calm. Confirm.
The goddess is addressed as 'Durga' in Shumbha's taunt; confirm the name in that verse.
Two readings of the line are attributed to teachers without ranking; confirm they are fair.
Devanagari for ekaivāhaṃ jagaty atra (एकैवाहं जगत्यत्र) and the pronunciation: confirm.
The goddesses are named generically (Brahmani, the boar-faced, the lion-faced); 'the goddess of Shiva's trident' stands for Maheshvari. Confirm.

Editor pass: the text says the goddesses headed by Brahmani entered her; 'Kali herself' was cut from the list as not certain. 'All week' (the breath-troops were last week) became 'all along'. 'The many were always one' was the narrator stating doctrine; now attributed to her words. The gather-the-scattered-parts practice and carry repeated 1054's gathering practice; replaced with a practice and carry drawn from the calm after Shumbha falls (rivers in their courses).
